rules_evaluated.rule_lead: Meta-frame lectures are closers, not openers.
rules_evaluated.fix_hint: This file is a pre-exercise prework/opener (arms with two cases before the Hallucination benchmark exercise), not a meta-frame lecture naming a pattern the student already lived — rule targets the other direction.

rules_evaluated.evidence: Lines 43-48 ('## Why the LLM fabricates') now carry four lenses (completes the shape / fills gaps instead of stopping / verifies inside the same fiction / inherits organisational shortcuts), lines 50-54 ('## Why grounding fails even when the facts are in context') carry three lenses — down from the prior six+four causal taxonomy. Each bullet is one line plus a short gloss, not a mapped-framework explanation. The prework arms the two-case read; the lecture owns the why.' This matches the rule's ARMS test (spirit + diagnostic lens + one operational primitive) rather than TEACHES (mapping frameworks, explaining tradeoffs with reasons).

stealing_the_mood: Teaching-moment fragility (not a mood-score dip, recorded here per template guidance since it has no check_strategy_tie_in rule_index): the homework asks the student to name 'the organisational check that would have caught this' in their own words for each case, but both cases already state that exact check verbatim in-body ('The missing check: one human opening the cited cases...' line 21; 'The missing check at Deloitte was not exotic: a reviewer opening each cited source...' line 37). A persona of any skill level can satisfy the close by paraphrasing a sentence already handed to them rather than deriving it from the case narrative — this is copy-work risk, not synthesis. UNCHANGED from the prior REVISE pass: the 2026-08-03 revision (commit 5fc7188) trimmed the mechanism sections (fixing check_lectures §2/§5 and strategy §4's front-run facet) but did not touch this. Fix belongs to the author (content-creation): state the case facts without naming the check, and let 'name the missing check' be the first place the answer appears in the student's own words.
